extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, academic researchers, and readers interested in journal governance and publishing ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Reporting and evaluation of editorial governance, policy changes, and integrity concerns for an academic mathematics journal. Focuses on conflicts between an editorial board and a commercial publisher over special issues, open access/APC policies, publication volume, and editorial control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific integrity over financial gain
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes the publisher wanted to make to the journal “would have the effect of jeopardizing scientific integrity for the sake of financial gain.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors resigned because proposed operational/editorial policies were viewed as incompatible with maintaining the highest standards of quality and academic integrity for the community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consultation and editorial control of special issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Special issues should not be introduced without consultation with, nor control from, the Editor-in-Chief nor the Editorial Board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The editorial board objects to publisher-introduced special issues 'with no consultation with, nor control from, the Editor-in-Chief nor the Editorial Board.' Special issues should be previously approved and curated by the board.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable publication volume targets
rubrics_metrics.description: Publication volume targets must be commensurate with quality; arbitrary large increases (e.g., five-fold) are problematic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publisher demanded increasing number of published papers five-fold (targeting ~100 papers from ~20), which editors saw as incompatible with maintaining quality and prestige.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial independence in referee selection and peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: It must be the editors and editorial board who indicate referees for each paper and control the peer-review process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: De Leon: 'it must be us, with the help of the EB members, who indicate the referees for each paper.' Allowing publisher staff to select referees undermines editorial standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overly short submission-to-publication cycles that harm quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Targeting an extremely fast cycle (e.g., two months from submission to publication) pressures editors to sacrifice editorial rigor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors perceived the two-month period for submission to publication as 'pressure to sacrifice the integrity of the editorial process to increase the number of accepted papers.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit non-specialist publisher staff control over editorial decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-specialist in-house staff editors should not be given substantive control over publication decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complaint that AIMS was giving non-specialist staff editors some control over publications; board requested that staff act under editorial direction rather than independently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open access APC policies must not exclude authors who lack funds
rubrics_metrics.description: Open access with author fees should not prevent quality papers from being published because authors cannot pay APCs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: De Leon emphasized 'that no quality paper cannot be published because the authors do not have the funds to pay the [open access fee].' Publisher offered APC waivers in some cases (e.g., recruited papers, special issues).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of APC waivers to protect submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: APC waiver policies (e.g., waiving fees for papers recruited by board members or special issues) can mitigate OA cost barriers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hu: 'all papers recruited by any board member will be APC waived; all special issues papers arranged by any board members will be APC waived.' Such policies are presented as partial solutions to equity concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency about journal identity and continuity after ownership/board changes
rubrics_metrics.description: When a journal changes title, scope, publisher, or editorial board, there should be clear communication about whether it is a continuation of the prior journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After resignations the old Journal of Geometric Mechanics was renamed Communications in Analysis and Mechanics with a new editorial board, raising questions about on what grounds it is a continuation of the previous title.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timely communication and clear governance procedures between publisher and editors
rubrics_metrics.description: Publisher and editorial board must communicate efficiently and agree on governance procedures, with timely responses and clarity on responsibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publisher insisted staff need 'instructions and feedback from the board in days, not weeks.' Editors sought meetings/Zoom calls to clarify future operation; poor communication preceded resignations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial board composition changes should be consensual
rubrics_metrics.description: Significant expansion or replacement of an editorial board should involve the existing board and not be imposed unilaterally by the publisher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors objected to being told to increase the board/five-fold number of published papers; after resignations the journal has a new editorial board, indicating contested governance over composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve established disciplinary standards and procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should follow 'the usual standards in mathematics journals'—longstanding review and editorial procedures that underpin prestige and trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: De Leon: without these standards 'the JGM cannot be continued.' Editors feared losing years of reputation if procedures were changed to prioritize quantity or speed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance financial sustainability with editorial standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers may argue for changes (e.g., move to OA, increase volume) on sustainability grounds; such financial considerations should be balanced against editorial integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publisher cited low subscriptions (<10), few articles published (~20/year), and the need to follow OA trends to make the journal sustainable; editors contested that such changes jeopardize quality.
